title: Knowledge Graph Specification

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.html:
This document fixes the shape of CHOIR's knowledge store. It derives three requirements — statement-level metadata, edges as edge targets, and native n-ary relations — assesses RDF triples, labelled property graphs, hypergraphs, semantic networks and knowledge graph embeddings against them, and decides on a typed, directed, role-labelled hypergraph as the model of record with an LPG projection and an RDF-star export (§1–§3). It specifies node and hyperedge schemas, an index set chosen for rule matching, and twelve machine-checkable store invariants (§4–§6).

The source carries the status "Draft for review". This publication is Active: the research document is drafted but not accepted as specification. choir/research/README.md records the programme-level position — "All 18 deliverables drafted. None accepted. Every document is a hypothesis, per MANIFESTO.md" — where MANIFESTO.md itself states the underlying formulation as "[t]reat every computational object as a hypothesis rather than an established truth". The source document itself does not cite MANIFESTO.md for its own status. It records that it "only fixes the shape" (§4.3), that physical realisation is "[n]ot decided here" (§8), and — in its single citation of MANIFESTO.md, which is to scope — that "implementation is deliberately deferred" (§8).

sections.heading: Research Question
sections.html: The source does not label a research question in a dedicated section. Its own framing, stated at the head of §1, is: "Before comparing storage models, state the requirement that eliminates most of them." The document therefore sets out to determine which storage model CHOIR's knowledge graph should use, by first deriving the requirements that decide the question and then assessing the candidate models against them. §9 restates the same question in the form of its answer: "Three requirements decide the model."

sections.heading: Finding
sections.html:
The three deciding requirements (§1)

The source takes two mandatory structures from reasoning_ontology.md §4.2 and a third from computational_primitives.md §3.6:

  1. Every relationship instance carries metadata — confidence, provenance, context, temporal validity. The source stresses the distinction: "Not the relationship type; every individual instance."
  2. Relationships can be targets of other relationships. "An undercutting defeater attacks an inference link. An influence edge modulates another edge's weight."
  3. Relations are natively n-ary. A śāstric rule condition such as "Jupiter in a kendra counted from the Moon, in a night birth, unaspected by Saturn" is "a single relational fact with four arguments plus a reference frame." Decomposing it into binary edges "does not merely add nodes — it destroys the fact that these arguments belong to one assertion, which is precisely what the rule matches on."

The stated consequence: any storage model that cannot do all three natively forces an encoding workaround, "and the workaround will leak into every query, every rule, and every explanation."

Candidate assessment (§2)

ModelVerdict as recorded in the source
RDF triples (+ OWL) (§2.1)"Excellent as an interchange format. Poor as a working store"
Labelled property graph (§2.2)"Excellent as a traversal and query projection. Insufficient as the model of record"
Hypergraph (§2.3)"Correct as the model of record"
Semantic networks (§2.4)"Not a candidate; a cautionary requirement"
Knowledge graph embeddings (§2.5)Retrieval only; "Embeddings may propose. They may never conclude."

RDF (§2.1). The source credits RDF with genuine standards, "[d]ecidable description-logic reasoning over a well-understood fragment", SPARQL, tooling and vocabulary reuse, and formal semantics, so that "what the graph entails" is a defined question — a property "which almost nothing else can say". The disqualifying weakness is reification: a triple has no identity. Four workarounds are assessed. Standard reification costs four extra triples per statement, "[a] 5× blow-up, and the reified statement is not asserted, so entailment does not flow through it." Named graphs/quads are workable for context but "one slot cannot carry confidence and provenance and validity interval independently." Singleton properties "[e]xplode… the vocabulary and break… schema reasoning." RDF-star / SPARQL-star is called "the modern answer" — it "genuinely fixes requirement 1 and largely fixes requirement 2", with the caveat that "[i]ts semantics are newer and support is less uniform than plain RDF", making it "the strongest RDF-family option." n-ary is not native; the standard workaround is an intermediate event node, "exactly the manual reification that requirement 3 says we will be doing constantly." The verdict rests on the observation that CHOIR's dominant operation — attaching and querying statement-level metadata — "is the operation RDF makes most awkward."

Labelled property graph (§2.2). Requirement 1 is "native and free"; traversal performance is excellent "and traversal is what rule matching mostly is." Four weaknesses are recorded. It has no formal semantics — "'What does this graph entail' has no standard answer. Any inference is application code." The source treats this as an acknowledged cost rather than a disqualifier on its own, noting the semantics burden lands on CHOIR "which, as it turns out, is where we want it anyway (§4.3), but it must be a conscious choice." Edges cannot be edge endpoints, so requirement 2 fails; n-ary needs an intermediate node, so requirement 3 fails; and property values are typically flat, so "nested metadata gets serialised into strings, which then cannot be queried."

Hypergraph (§2.3). All three requirements are met: requirement 3 natively (the four-argument condition becomes one hyperedge with roles {subject: Guru, frame: Candra, region: kendra, qualifier: night-birth}); requirement 1 natively "if hyperedges have identity, which in any practical encoding they do"; and requirement 2 follows, since "a hyperedge with identity can be a participant in another hyperedge." The source adds a domain-specific argument: "Role-labelling aligns exactly with kāraka analysis." Pāṇini's kāraka system assigns semantic roles (agent, locus, source, instrument) to participants in a single action, so "[a] kāraka-analysed śloka is a role-labelled hyperedge", making the mapping from sanskrit_analysis_pipeline.md §6 to storage "near-mechanical rather than a lossy translation." The recorded weaknesses are not minor: "Fewer off-the-shelf engines. No standard query language. Formal semantics must be supplied. Naive implementations have poor traversal locality."

Semantic networks (§2.4). Quillian and the frame systems are treated as the historical ancestor whose durable contributions — inheritance hierarchies, typed links, spreading activation — are already absorbed into the other models. Their known failure, "diagnosed by Woods in What's in a Link?", is named as the one CHOIR must avoid: "link types with no defined semantics." This is why reasoning_ontology.md §4.1 forces every relation to declare arity, transitivity, symmetry and inverse.

Embeddings and the neural/symbolic boundary (§2.5). Embeddings are credited with approximate retrieval, candidate generation, fuzzy paraphrase matching, suggesting plausible missing links, and clustering near-duplicate rules across recensions. What they cannot do is "[j]ustify anything": an embedding score "is not evidence in the sense of computational_primitives.md §3.11 — it has no source, no derivation, and no defeater structure. It cannot be traced, and it cannot be explained beyond 'the vectors were close.'" The source states the boundary as a hard rule:

Neural retrieval, symbolic adjudication. Embeddings may propose. They may never conclude.

Permitted: candidate generation, deduplication proposals, search ranking, alignment suggestions, anomaly flagging for human review. Forbidden: contributing to a confidence score, satisfying a rule condition, resolving a conflict, or appearing in an explanation as a reason.

Anything an embedding surfaces enters the graph only after a symbolic or human check and carries provenance recording that its origin was a retrieval suggestion. Without this line, traceability (001 §3.16) "fails silently — the worst failure mode, because the system still produces confident-looking explanations."

The decision (§3)

A hypergraph of record — typed, directed, n-ary, role-labelled participants, statement-level metadata, immutable and versioned — with, in the source's own count, two projections: an LPG projection for traversal and rule matching, and an RDF-star export for interoperability and external reasoners. The §3 diagram places a third derived store alongside them — a vector index for retrieval only — and marks all three "derived, rebuildable".

"Only the hypergraph is authoritative. Projections are caches: derivable, disposable, rebuildable. No conclusion may depend on a projection-only fact."

The source argues against itself before concluding. It asks "Why not just use RDF-star and skip the layer?" and answers that RDF-star "is the closest alternative and a defensible choice", losing native n-ary role-labelling (requirement 3) — "the requirement most tied to the Sanskrit pipeline." The layered design keeps RDF-star as an export target "so the interoperability benefit is retained without paying the encoding cost on every write." Projection lag must be explicit: a projection carries the version of the record graph it was built from, and queries against a stale projection are detectable.

Schemas (§4)

The Node schema (§4.1) carries id (ContentAddress or NominalID), kind, class, multilingual labels (IAST, Devanāgarī, English), attributes (definitional only, per 001 §3.3), provenance, created, version, supersedes and status. The source draws attention to an omission: "no state field. States are time-indexed and therefore modelled as hyperedges with validity intervals, not as node properties. Putting mutable state on nodes is the single most common way graph systems lose their temporal audit trail."

The Hyperedge schema (§4.2) is called "the unit that matters". It carries relation (from the seven families), participants as {role, target, optional} where target may be a NodeID or a HyperedgeID, arity, polarity, modality (asserts|indicates|obliges|permits|forbids|requires), the context reference, three time fields (valid_time, decision_time, transaction_time), confidence marked "DERIVED, never authored", provenance, evidence, defeated_by ("marked, never deleted"), derives_from (the traceability closure), version and status.

The source justifies each field against a named requirement:

FieldRequired by
participants[].roleKāraka mapping (005 §6); n-ary requirement
target: HyperedgeIDSecond-order influence & undercutting defeat (002 §4.2)
contextContradiction tolerance (001 §3.10)
Three time fieldsTri-temporal audit (001 §3.17)
confidenceThree-axis model (011)
defeated_byNon-destruction invariant (001 §3.11)
derives_fromTraceability invariant (001 §3.16)
modalityDeontic domains; normative constraints (001 §3.9)

Semantics are an acknowledged debt (§4.3). "Choosing a hypergraph means no inherited formal semantics." The obligation is discharged elsewhere — in reasoning_language.md §7, which fixes the entailment relation over this structure (defeasible, non-monotonic, with a well-founded defeater ordering). "This document only fixes the shape; the meaning is specified there. Storing without defined semantics is the Woods failure of §2.4 and is not acceptable."

Indexing (§5)

Indexes are chosen for rule matching, "not analytics": class extension (class → nodes), role-participation ((relation, role, target) → hyperedges), context, a temporal interval tree over valid_time (serving daśā windows among others), provenance (source_locus → objects), content address (dedup and independent-attestation detection), defeater (target → exceptions), and a vector index marked "Retrieval only (§2.5)". The role-participation index is identified as the hot path: "rule conditions are patterns over (relation, role, target) triples, and matching is intersection over these postings lists."

Invariants (§6)

Twelve machine-checkable invariants, stated as the properties the store must maintain and intended to populate the currently empty choir/ontology/relationship_validation.md:

#InvariantRationale
I1Nodes and hyperedges are immutable once written; change = new version + supersedesHistorical re-derivability (002 §7.3)
I2Every hyperedge has a non-empty contextNo context-free assertions (001 §3.10)
I3Every hyperedge has provenance naming a source or a kernelNo fact without an origin
I4confidence is present only where a derivation exists; never hand-setConfidence is computed (001 §3.14)
I5Defeated objects are marked, never removedNon-destruction (001 §3.11)
I6derives_from closure is acyclicTraceability terminates
I7subclass-of and part-of closures are acyclicOntology check V8
I8Every participant role is declared legal for that relation typeWoods requirement
I9No conclusion's derives_from closure contains a vector-index objectNeural/symbolic boundary (§2.5)
I10Projections declare the record-graph version they were built fromStale-read detection
I11Arity matches the relation's declarationSchema integrity
I12valid_time ⊆ the context's temporal scopeContexts bound their contents

The source singles out I9 as fragile in practice: "It is easy to state and easy to violate accidentally the first time someone wants 'just a little' similarity in a score."

Worked example (§7)

The core Gajakesarī condition — Jupiter situated in a kendra counted from the Moon — is encoded both ways. As binary triples it takes six triples plus an intermediate node, "and the fact that these belong to one assertion is implicit"; the source annotates the RDF sketch with "# confidence? provenance? context? → reify again, or lose them". As one role-labelled hyperedge the assertion is a single object with metadata attached directly: relation choir:core/PositionalRelation#occupies-region, arity 3, modality indicates, context ctx:{ tradition: parāśara, chart: rāśi, application: jātaka }, and participants

  • kartṛ → jyotisha:graha/Guru (the situated one)
  • adhikaraṇa → jyotisha:region/Kendra (the locus)
  • apādāna → jyotisha:graha/Candra (the reckoning point)

"The roles are the kāraka labels recovered by the Sanskrit pipeline: kartṛ (agent / situated entity), adhikaraṇa (locus), apādāna (point of reckoning, realised by the ablative candrāt). The grammatical analysis survives into storage rather than being flattened away — which is what makes the explanation able to say why the Moon is the reference frame and not the subject." The example is developed fully in canonical_shloka_analysis.md.

sections.heading: Architectural Implications
sections.html:
The source names the DAALE boundaries it touches: daale/ontology/relationships.py and evidence.py.

  • Single source of truth. Only the hypergraph is authoritative; the LPG projection, the RDF-star export and the vector index are caches. No conclusion may depend on a projection-only fact (§3). Invariant I10 makes projection lag detectable rather than silent.
  • CHOIR must supply its own formal semantics. The choice of a hypergraph forfeits any inherited entailment relation. The source records this as a non-optional debt discharged in reasoning_language.md §7 (§4.3, §9), not as something this document settles.
  • Kāraka analysis survives into storage. Role-labelled participants mean the grammatical analysis produced by sanskrit_analysis_pipeline.md §6 is preserved rather than flattened, "which is what keeps grammatical justification available at explanation time" (§9).
  • A hard neural/symbolic boundary. Embeddings propose, never conclude; enforced by invariant I9 (§2.5, §9). Anything an embedding surfaces requires a symbolic or human check and carries provenance recording its retrieval origin.
  • Time and state modelling. States are hyperedges with validity intervals, not node properties (§4.1), and every hyperedge carries three time fields for tri-temporal audit (001 §3.17).
  • Non-destruction and traceability become storage-level checks. I5 (defeated objects marked, never removed) and I6 (derives_from closure acyclic) turn the invariants of 001 §3.11 and §3.16 into machine-checkable acceptance criteria on the store (§6).
  • Indexing follows rule matching, not analytics (§5), with (relation, role, target) as the core match primitive.

sections.heading: Open Questions
sections.html:
The source records five open items (§8), plus further unresolved matter elsewhere:

  1. Physical realisation. A hypergraph can be implemented over a relational store, an LPG with a strict reification convention, or a dedicated engine. "Not decided here; the logical model is the commitment, and per MANIFESTO.md scope, implementation is deliberately deferred."
  2. Context inheritance in queries. Whether a query scoped to a specific context should automatically see facts from more general contexts (lattice-upward closure) is "a semantics question with real performance consequences. Deferred to reasoning_language.md."
  3. Content addressing and near-duplicates. Hashing canonical form unifies exact restatements; paraphrases across recensions will not unify. Whether normalisation should be aggressive enough to unify them — "at the risk of merging genuinely different rules — is unresolved, and interacts with rule_extraction_framework.md §7."
  4. Retraction versus defeat. I5 forbids deletion, but a rule extracted in error (a mis-parse, not a defeat) differs from a rule defeated by an exception. "Both are currently status values; whether they need different machinery is open."
  5. Projection consistency model. Whether projections must be transactionally consistent with the record graph or may be eventually consistent "affects whether a rule match can observe a torn state."

Additionally recorded as unsettled or as costs carried forward: the formal semantics of the store are not fixed by this document and remain owed to reasoning_language.md §7 (§4.3); hypergraphs have "[f]ewer off-the-shelf engines[,] [n]o standard query language" and "[n]aive implementations have poor traversal locality" (§2.3); RDF-star's "semantics are newer and support is less uniform than plain RDF" (§2.1); and invariant I9 "is the one that requires ongoing vigilance" (§6). The source's own status line reads "Draft for review", and the document validates no claim empirically — it presents a design decision and its justification, with the worked example (§7) as illustration rather than measurement.
